doc: Why a demand the guest's I/O queue started did not deliver.
The host runs the transport and is the one that catches an exception, so
it is the one that knows which of these happened; what crosses is the
number. The prose a browser writes for a failed request ("TypeError:
Failed to fetch") is the host's own, and there is nothing the guest can
do with it that it cannot do with this — it neither retries on it nor
routes by it, it only tells one failure from another, which a number does.
A refusal keeps the host's own number beside this rather than inside it:
folding it in would make one reason per code, and the guest routes by
neither.
The number is the name: an old host reads a number a new guest sends, so
a number that has meant something must never come to mean another thing.
Retire one by leaving the gap.
name: FetchFail

entries.name: None
doc: It did not fail.

entries.name: Network
doc: The transport itself failed — offline, DNS, CORS, a refused
connection. `TypeError` is what a browser raises for all of them.

entries.name: Shell
doc: The host raised something else. Its own words say what; the guest
only needs to count it apart from the rest.

entries.section: 0x02 a response arrived and was not usable

entries.name: Refused
doc: The host answered, and not with the object. `detail` carries whatever
number it refused with, which for HTTP is the status.

entries.name: NoRoom
doc: The guest had no room for the body it was offered.

entries.section: 0x03 the bytes arrived and did not hold up

entries.name: Decode
doc: The body did not decode as its format.

retired: 0x0302 and 0x0303 are retired. They named a key with no page and a key
with no category, and neither side ever raised one: the host is handed
a key it was given and hands it back, and the guest looks the key up
before it starts a demand at all, so by the time a body has arrived
there is nothing left to be wrong about. The numbers stay taken.
